children: HSBC Global Research remains bullish on the global artificial intelligence
trade but warned that its next phase depends on concrete evidence that corporate monetization can keep pace with massive hyperscaler
capital expenditures.
Monetization progress & budget runway
Revenue drivers for frontier AI models show substantial momentum. Anthropic
reached an annualized revenue run rate of $65B as of July, while OpenAI

hit $40B, according to the HSBC note citing Bloomberg and Reuters data. Corporate adoption, however, remains in early innings. Ramp AI data show the median company spends just $12 per month per employee on AI models, while the top 10% spends $650 per month—both figures accelerating sharply.
Corporate budgets appear large enough to support materially higher AI spending. If the average S&P 500

company spent $650 per employee per month, annual spending would reach $250B—equivalent to just 5% of S&P 500 EBITDA, 8% of wages, and 27% of research and development. AI accounts for just 20% of software budgets, but that is shifting rapidly, with 50% of new information technology and software
budgets now being allocated to AI.

Improving model capability should expand the amount companies are willing to pay. METR data show the Claude Mythos model has an 80% success rate at tasks lasting over three hours—Claude Opus, released in May 2025, achieved a similar success rate only on tasks lasting 20 minutes. This progression from assisting with individual prompts to executing end-to-end workflows expands both the addressable market and the value against which companies can justify spending.
Hyperscaler capex and the FCF gap

The capital investment landscape presents a timing challenge. Consensus expects U.S. hyperscaler capex to reach $770B in 2026 and $1.1T in 2027, with estimates revised up by $170B and $260B, respectively, since the start of the second-quarter earnings season. S&P Global Ratings estimates that U.S. hyperscalers will spend more than $7T on data centers and AI-related capex between 2025 and 2030, HSBC noted.

Free cash flow has already turned negative and is expected to remain under pressure until the end of 2027 as spending is incurred several years before the full revenue opportunity materializes. Hyperscalers are bridging that gap through external financing, with debt issuance reaching nearly $250B so far in 2026, plus more than $1T of uncommenced lease commitments.
Despite these pressures, demand signals remain strong. Remaining performance obligations across Microsoft
, Amazon
, Alphabet
, and Oracle
reached some $2.35T in the second quarter of 2026, up from $815B one year earlier. Rental prices for NVIDIA

B200 and H100 GPUs have continued to rise despite rapid capacity increases, suggesting usable compute remains scarce. HSBC expects hyperscaler return on invested capital will fall but remain sufficiently high at 17% by 2028.
Global portfolio positioning
HSBC's strategic recommendations tilt toward areas with the strongest demand and monetization outlook where valuations are not stretched, favoring emerging markets

—particularly Korean memory, Taiwan semiconductors and advanced packaging—as well as mainland China's semiconductor equipment and power infrastructure. These markets provide exposure where demand remains strong and capacity remains constrained, with generally less stretched valuations than parts of the U.S. AI complex.
Within the U.S., the bank prefers semiconductors

over hyperscalers over software, noting that semiconductor and cloud infrastructure companies retain direct exposure to rising training and inference volumes with revenues less dependent on which individual model ultimately wins. HSBC would fade the recent rotation into software, viewing it as driven more by short covering than a material improvement in underlying fundamentals.
